subtitle: Understand the meanings of disability that each person has learned, and offer support without turning culture, a diagnosis or appearance into a prediction about them.
scope: For staff across DHS examining how learned meanings can influence views of disability. Original practice adults supply different interpretations; none represents a cultural group or establishes a diagnosis, capacity decision or assessment orientation. WHO’s ICF overview provides context about functioning and environment, not a classroom diagnostic tool. Actual disability rights, access, employment, records and service responsibilities continue through their applicable processes. Learning is voluntary. Private reflection with the example is valid; no medical information, personal story or live case is required. Native American and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA.
introTranscript: People can learn different meanings of disability, care and participation. Those meanings can shape a first interpretation without defining what another person needs. Follow Ren’s practice request to contribute to a planning conversation, examine the views that staff bring and connect a wider understanding to an appropriate response. Keep actual responsibilities and unanswered conditions clear. Learn at your own pace and reflect privately if you prefer.

intro.heading: The request concerns a contribution
intro.body:
Disability can be part of a person’s experience without explaining every preference, ability or meaning. Staff bring learned ideas about disability to a conversation, and those ideas can shape what they notice. A useful beginning separates the person’s supplied account from the story a listener adds. This makes the actual question clearer without requiring a diagnosis or personal history.

In the example, Ren is an adult with low vision who wants to contribute observations about a proposed neighborhood walking route at a public planning conversation. Ren asks for the route description in a format that can be examined before the discussion. Staff member Iona initially suggests that Ren could skip the meeting to avoid strain. The response supplies a preference Ren has not expressed and leaves the requested information unanswered.

Ren’s purpose is contribution, not simply attendance. Ren wants to discuss a crossing and a rest point from personal observations. The actual access arrangements and the decision about the route remain unconfirmed in this learning case. Asking about usable information does not establish that every proposed suggestion will be adopted, but it deserves an accurate response through the relevant process.

The WHO ICF overview describes functioning and disability in context, including environmental factors. The limited point used here is that an account of disability should not ignore the task and surrounding conditions. This course does not teach ICF assessment, assign codes or decide Ren’s medical or legal status. The Council of Europe source also explains that meanings are personalized and contextual; a listener’s first interpretation is not automatically the person’s account.

A better next question might be, “Which route information would you like to examine, and what way of receiving it would be useful?” Staff can explain what is actually available and use the applicable access process for what still needs to be arranged. They should not promise effectiveness from the name of a feature or decide that nonattendance is the caring choice without Ren’s preference.

Privately examine the difference between Ren’s request and Iona’s initial response. You may recognize a familiar learned story of disability as withdrawal, protection or needing others to decide. Recognizing that interpretation does not make it a fact about Ren. You can use the example for learning; no medical records, live meeting or public disclosure is necessary.

items.title: Keep contribution visible
items.body: Ren wants to discuss a crossing and rest point. An attendance-only account could omit that contribution even if a meeting seat is offered. Ask what information supports the contribution rather than assume that being present or staying home is the whole decision.

items.title: Do not make protection the person’s preference
items.body: Iona’s concern about strain may be intended as care, but Ren has not chosen to withdraw. A useful response can ask about the task and support without deciding the person’s preferred participation from low vision. Actual safety and service responsibilities still need their relevant facts.

items.title: Preserve the access process
items.body: The course identifies a format question, not a completed accommodation or legal finding. Staff must use the process that actually applies. A learning answer cannot approve a particular tool or establish that an offered format is effective for Ren.

tabs.label: Disability as complete explanation
tabs.body: If low vision is treated as sufficient reason to skip the meeting, the response removes Ren’s expressed contribution before the actual information question is examined. A label may be relevant without determining the person’s preference or every task condition.

tabs.label: Attendance as complete answer
tabs.body: Offering a seat could be useful while leaving the route description unusable. Ren needs information for the contribution, not just a location in the room. Examine what the particular support makes possible rather than equate presence with meaningful participation.

tabs.label: Purpose and task clarified
tabs.body: Ren’s observations and requested information guide the next question. Staff can identify actual available support and the responsible process for unresolved needs. This preserves the contribution without promising adoption of Ren’s proposal or approval of every arrangement.

intro.heading: Care can mean easing a task or enabling a contribution
intro.body:
A staff member may understand disability support through personally learned experiences that differ from another person’s. Those meanings can be important without defining what everyone with a disability needs. Cultural learning asks people to recognize the meanings the people describe, compare them with their own and respond to the actual context. It should not replace one rigid view with another.

In the example, Iona describes volunteering at a recovery group where simplifying an optional activity and leaving time for rest expressed attentive care. Members had chosen that arrangement for the group’s purpose. Iona brings the learned meaning into Ren’s case and initially interprets removing the meeting task as the kinder response. The earlier group’s chosen practice does not establish Ren’s current preference.

Colleague Jase describes an adaptive sports club where preparing equipment together allowed members to contribute to a game. For Jase, support often expressed membership and participation rather than withdrawal from the task. Jase initially assumes that every offer of relief is less respectful. That also overextends a particular experience; someone can value rest or declining an activity without rejecting participation in life.

Ren supplies the relevant choice: “I want to make the route observations myself. I want the description in a way I can examine; I do not want someone to present my comments for me.” Iona can now understand that support may enable Ren’s contribution rather than spare Ren from it. Jase can retain the participation meaning without treating every requested break as a lesser choice. The staff response changes toward asking about usable information and Ren’s chosen role.

This is a genuine meaning contrast rather than a cultural-group profile. The Council of Europe source describes personalized affiliations and contextual perspective-taking. Iona’s and Jase’s experiences supply the learned meanings in the example; ethnicity, nationality or disability category does not supply them. The course does not infer anyone’s IDI orientation or judge which person is more developed.

You can reflect privately on what care or assistance first meant to you in this encounter. Understanding a different meaning does not require endorsing an exclusionary practice, copying another person’s experience or ignoring actual rights. It allows you to question a response that felt caring and ask how it fits the person’s own account. That private understanding is meaningful without a public story, medical disclosure or a live program change.

items.title: Understand Iona’s earlier setting
items.body: Rest and simpler activities mattered in a recovery group where members chose them. That experience can remain valuable. The overextension occurs when Iona assumes it decides what care should mean for Ren’s route contribution before asking.

items.title: Understand Jase without a new ranking
items.body: Equipment preparation expressed membership in the sports club. It offers a useful alternative meaning of support. It does not establish that everyone must prefer active contribution at every moment or that choosing rest is evidence of a lesser perspective.

items.title: Change the actual response
items.body: Ren wants to examine information and present observations personally. Asking about usable information preserves that stated role. The response changes because support is understood as enabling this contribution, not because staff decide that one personal history should become a universal rule.

tabs.label: Care as relief
tabs.body: Iona learned that reducing an optional task could recognize a person’s recovery needs. Transferring that meaning without checking Ren could remove a valued contribution. Clarify the preference instead of assuming that the earlier chosen arrangement answers this new situation.

tabs.label: Care as participation
tabs.body: Jase learned that prepared equipment helped people contribute to a shared game. This meaning can widen Iona’s reading of support. It becomes another rigid view if Jase treats every declined task or request for rest as a failure to participate.

tabs.label: Person’s chosen contribution
tabs.body: Ren asks for a usable description while retaining the speaking role. The next response should examine that actual need through its process. Chosen support, relief and independent action are not ranks; their fit depends on the person’s account and actual conditions.

check.question: Which response follows the widened understanding?
check.correct: Ask about usable information for Ren’s chosen contribution without imposing withdrawal or a universal participation rule.
wrong: Remove the task because Iona’s earlier group valued rest.
Require active participation because Jase’s club valued contribution.
Assign an intercultural stage from the two histories.
check.feedbackCorrect: This uses the meaning contrast to respond to Ren’s actual preference without ranking people or activities.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Imposed withdrawal treats one learned care meaning as universal. Compulsory activity treats the other meaning as superior even when a person chooses differently. A stage assignment is an unsupported assessment from a learning case. The actual request, not either rule, should guide the response.

items.text: Chosen rest expressed care in Iona’s earlier group.
Prepared equipment expressed participation in Jase’s club.
Clarify the description Ren wants to examine.
Preserve Ren’s chosen speaking role through the applicable process.
Every person with low vision should avoid the task.
Every rest request shows a lower perspective.

intro.heading: Ren can choose what to share
intro.body:
A meaning supplied by one person can widen your understanding without becoming a prediction about others. Iona and Jase described particular settings and their own interpretations. Their accounts help explain their first responses, but neither account determines what Ren believes about disability. Curiosity remains useful when it allows another person to choose how much to share.

In the example, Iona begins to understand that removing the task might not express care for Ren. Iona then asks whether Ren’s family usually expects others to speak for a person with low vision. Ren declines to discuss family views and returns to the route description: “I want to examine the crossing information myself.” That response supplies a present preference without supplying a family history.

A respectful next step accepts the boundary. Iona can say, “You do not need to explain that history. Let us focus on the route information and your contribution.” This does not abandon intercultural learning. Iona can privately examine why a family explanation seemed necessary and how disability had become a complete story in the first interpretation. The learning belongs to Iona without turning Ren into a required source of personal instruction.

Jase also needs to keep the earlier sports-club experience in context. It does not establish that every person with low vision prefers the same support or that someone declining this meeting is less interested in community life. Another person could have a different purpose, schedule or chosen way of participating. An unanswered preference requires an appropriate question, not a group prediction.

The Council of Europe source describes culture through personalized affiliations and context rather than treating individuals as identical representatives. The relevant lesson is not that every person must explain those affiliations. Understanding can begin with your own assumptions and the individually supplied meaning that someone freely offers. The person’s actual request, rights and service responsibilities do not depend on giving a cultural account.

Use the example privately if you prefer. You can recognize the limit of the family question and prepare a response that keeps the practical matter moving. Do not infer shame, agreement, resistance, family control or lack of trust from Ren’s declined sharing. Those explanations remain unknown. Actual information requirements of a relevant process must still be explained accurately; this course does not waive them or create a new medical inquiry.

lessons.keyStatement: A declined story is a boundary, not evidence of a hidden preference.

items.title: Notice what Ren answered
items.body: Ren clarified the wish to examine the crossing information and declined family discussion. Those are two distinct parts of the response. Staff can use the supplied task preference while leaving the family meaning unknown.

items.title: Examine your own question
items.body: Iona can ask privately why a family explanation seemed necessary to respond. This can reveal a learned assumption that disability choices must be explained by others. The reflection is useful even if Ren never supplies a personal story.

items.title: Explain actual information needs accurately
items.body: A relevant process may require particular task information or appropriate documentation within actual authority. Explain that requirement and its responsible role rather than attach an optional cultural-history demand. The course does not establish that all later process information is unnecessary.

tabs.label: Invite an account
tabs.body: An optional invitation allows Ren to decide whether an account is useful. If Ren declines, the route-information request remains. The invitation should not carry an implied penalty or suggest that the person must teach staff before receiving a response.

tabs.label: Demand a representative story
tabs.body: A family or community explanation can become a condition of help if staff keep asking after it is declined. It also risks treating Ren as a representative of others. The practical task does not require staff to establish a cultural profile.

tabs.label: Reflect and continue
tabs.body: Iona can reconsider the assumption privately and return to Ren’s supplied purpose. This changes staff behavior without claiming to know a hidden family meaning. Actual support arrangements still require their relevant process and confirmation.

check.question: What should Iona do after Ren declines the family discussion?
check.correct: Respect the boundary, reconsider the question privately and continue the actual information request through its process.
wrong: Infer that Ren’s family opposes participation.
Require a community explanation before answering the format question.
Treat declined sharing as proof that Ren distrusts all staff.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response preserves the supplied preference and keeps unanswered meanings unknown without withholding the actual task response.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The family-opposition conclusion invents a meaning Ren did not supply. Requiring a community explanation turns personal instruction into a gate to help. A broad distrust conclusion exceeds the declined question. Respecting the boundary allows staff learning and the actual request to continue.

intro.heading: A usable description supports a specific contribution
intro.body:
A disability label does not tell staff whether information in a particular form supports a particular task. The WHO ICF overview describes functioning and disability in context and includes environmental factors. This course uses that limited context point to examine a task; it does not train clinical assessment or assign functioning scores. Ren’s own account is needed to understand what the information should make possible.

In the example, Ren wants to examine the crossing and rest-point descriptions before offering observations. A staff member says that a larger-print handout has been prepared, while another suggests an audio description. Neither proposed feature establishes that Ren can examine the relevant information in time or navigate it for the intended contribution. Staff need to explain what is actually available and receive Ren’s account of usefulness.

Ren asks to compare the two descriptions beforehand and says that the crossing’s location and the relation to the rest point are important. This clarifies the task without supplying a full medical history. The actual availability, timing and effectiveness remain unconfirmed. A useful response identifies the responsible access process and explains the next arrangement rather than claim that the phrase “large print” or “audio” settles the issue.

Timing is also part of the task. Information that arrives after the conversation may not support the intended opportunity to examine it beforehand. That is a task-specific observation, not an invented universal deadline. Staff should confirm the actual requirements and arrangements instead of promise a classroom-created schedule or disregard a current access need until a learning review is finished.

Suppose Ren can identify the rest point in one offered description but cannot locate the crossing in that same description. The supplied observation would support a question about that information condition. It would not establish that Ren lacks the ability to understand routes or that all formats fail. Conversely, one successful task would not establish that every later participation condition is resolved.

Privately map the purpose, information condition and unanswered question. You can learn from the example without testing a person or collecting diagnostic information. Staff’s actual legal, technical and service responsibilities continue through their relevant routes. An environment inquiry should support participation and accurate understanding, not become a new ability test or a shortcut to approving an unverified arrangement.

accordion.heading: Examine conditions without a capacity judgment

items.title: Connect information to purpose
items.body: The crossing and rest-point relationship is the relevant content in this case. A general assurance that the handout is improved might leave that task unanswered. Ask which content and route are useful rather than treat a feature label as a complete result.

items.title: Confirm the arrangement honestly
items.body: The print and audio ideas are proposals until their availability and fit are established through the actual process. Explain what is confirmed, what remains open and who can respond. This avoids turning a good intention into a false promise.

items.title: Keep observations within their scope
items.body: Difficulty locating a crossing in one description can identify a condition to examine. It does not establish overall intelligence, motivation or capacity. A useful observation remains tied to the actual task and avoids a diagnosis from behavior.

tabs.label: Feature offered
tabs.body: A larger-print handout may be a useful option, but its name does not explain whether the needed relationship is understandable or available beforehand. Staff should identify its actual content and receive task-specific feedback within the applicable process.

tabs.label: Effect described
tabs.body: Ren’s account that the rest point is clear while the crossing remains difficult gives more specific information. It can guide a revision or another support question. It does not settle every access arrangement or establish a broad legal conclusion.

tabs.label: Capacity inferred
tabs.body: If staff conclude that Ren cannot understand routes from one information difficulty, the environment has disappeared from the explanation. The inference exceeds the supplied observation. Return to the task condition and actual responsibilities instead of make a complete ability judgment.

check.question: What does a proposed larger-print handout establish at this point?
check.correct: A possible information option whose actual availability and usefulness for Ren’s task still need confirmation.
wrong: Complete effective access because the feature has a name.
Ren’s inability to understand routes if one section remains unclear.
A universal deadline created by this course.
check.feedbackCorrect: This keeps the proposal separate from its actual task effect and relevant process requirements.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A feature name does not prove that the needed information is usable. One unclear section does not establish complete capacity. The course does not create a universal timing rule; the actual task and applicable requirements need an accurate response.

intro.heading: Understanding is not an excuse or an approval
intro.body:
Understanding how a staff member learned a meaning can improve the response without making every resulting action acceptable. Iona’s earlier experience helps explain why relieving a task initially seemed caring. It does not authorize excluding Ren from an opportunity because of a disability label. The relevant rights and access responsibilities must remain part of the response, not be postponed until a cultural conversation feels complete.

The current posted public-entity rule at 28 CFR 35.130 prohibits disability discrimination within its scope and addresses equal opportunity, reasonable modifications and legitimate safety requirements. Its safety requirements must be based on actual risks rather than speculation, stereotypes or generalizations about disability. This course does not make a legal determination about Ren’s case, approve every requested arrangement or substitute this public-entity rule for employment accommodation procedures. Staff should use the actual applicable process and responsible authority.

Consider a separate practice employment example. Employee Beau says that, because of low vision, a changed information format is needed to perform a work task. Ordinary words can identify an initial accommodation request; a special legal phrase is not required. Under MMB Policy 1433, the recipient promptly forwards the request to the appropriate decision maker and simultaneously informs Beau who that person is. Actual agency delegation determines the decision-making role. The agency ADA Coordinator handles requests outside supervisors’ or managers’ actual delegated authority and provides appropriate consultation.

Supervisors and managers must not request medical information or documentation. Any appropriate request belongs to the agency ADA Coordinator under the policy’s procedures. This is separate from explaining the work task or relevant functions. Personal cultural reflection also does not justify collecting a medical or family history. Protect actual need-to-know information and use the relevant agency process.

In another practice example, supervisor Yara hears an allegation that disability-based comments were used to deny a staff opportunity. MMB Policy 1436 requires managers and supervisors immediately to report protected-class allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow actual agency procedures. Optional teamwork or intercultural learning cannot become a proof threshold or waiting period. Assigned investigation and corrective-action responsibilities remain governed by actual procedures and authority.

You may examine these distinctions privately using the example. The course makes no finding about an actual person or agency event and imposes no live work product. The learning question is how a broader interpretation informs behavior while actual responsibilities continue. A respectful explanation, an appropriate referral and an honest account of what remains open can work together; cultural understanding is neither an excuse for harm nor a new source of formal authority.

items.title: Do not turn care into exclusion
items.body: Iona can recognize a well-intended earlier meaning while changing the response to Ren’s expressed contribution. Understanding the intention does not establish that removing the opportunity is lawful or effective. The relevant access and decision processes still apply.

items.title: Route the employment request accurately
items.body: Beau’s disability-related need for a changed work format should be recognized and promptly forwarded to the appropriate decision maker, with simultaneous notice identifying that person. Actual delegation matters. Supervisors/managers do not acquire medical-documentation authority because they received the initial request.

items.title: Preserve immediate reporting
items.body: Yara must immediately report the protected-class allegation to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow actual procedures. The course does not decide the allegation or ban properly assigned responsibilities. Optional learning may support understanding but cannot delay the required route.

tabs.label: Meaning understood
tabs.body: Iona’s recovery-group experience explains why relief felt caring. A wider interpretation now makes Ren’s chosen contribution visible. This understanding can change the response without excusing exclusion or promising that a particular support is already approved.

tabs.label: Actual process followed
tabs.body: Beau’s request and Yara’s reporting duty use their actual responsible routes. Forwarding and notice, appropriate documentation roles and immediate reporting are concrete responsibilities. They do not depend on producing a cultural story or finishing the course.

tabs.label: Finding not invented
tabs.body: A learning answer does not establish a violation, capacity judgment or completed accommodation. Staff must preserve the actual process and authority. Naming that limit should not be used to delay an appropriate response to a current need or allegation.

check.question: What is Yara’s appropriate response to the protected-class allegation as the supervisor?

wrong: Wait for a cultural learning conversation to establish agreement.
Require the employee to prove the allegation before reporting.
Assume this course authorizes an independently chosen investigation outside actual procedures.

intro.heading: Specific understanding can be enough
intro.body:
A useful review of learning can describe a particular interpretation that changed without claiming complete competence or an assessment result. Iona first understood care as removing a potentially difficult task. After receiving Ren’s actual preference and considering Jase’s different experience, Iona recognized that support could enable a valued contribution. The changed response asked about usable route information while preserving Ren’s chosen speaking role.

That is a meaningful learning account even if Iona keeps it private. It concerns a supplied meaning and a specific response, not a ranking of Iona, Jase or Ren. Jase also learned not to make every chosen break a lesser form of participation. The wider perspective does not turn active contribution, rest or independent action into a hierarchy of people.

In the original follow-up fiction, Ren says that a revised crossing description can now be examined for the intended comments. This supplies feedback about that information task. The planning conversation has not yet occurred, and the decision about the route remains open. Staff should not claim that the support caused an adopted proposal, that every meeting condition is resolved or that the course establishes legal compliance.

Two other offered information arrangements have no supplied feedback. Their usefulness remains unknown. Silence does not establish satisfaction, resistance, lack of ability or absence of an access concern. The actual staff role and applicable process determine appropriate follow-up; this course does not create a universal feedback schedule or permission to gather unnecessary personal information.

An accurate account might say, “I reconsidered a care meaning that initially removed the task. I changed the response toward Ren’s chosen contribution. Ren supplied useful feedback about the revised crossing description; the meeting and route decision are still open.” This preserves learning, task effect and uncertainty without adding a causal explanation. It also leaves actual access, employment or reporting responsibilities separate and active where they apply.

You can finish by reflecting privately on the example. Name what you now understand about disability, care or contribution that was less visible at first. If you later use an appropriate actual task, keep your authority, privacy and relevant responsibilities clear. No medical disclosure, live case, public proof or assessed orientation is required for completion. A specific changed understanding is worth recognizing without turning it into a claim that every future situation will be handled well.

items.title: Describe the particular understanding
items.body: Iona reconsidered whether care required removing Ren’s task. The changed response preserved contribution and examined support. This is more precise than a claim to have mastered all disability perspectives or an invented assessment stage.

items.title: Keep the effect with its task
items.body: Ren’s feedback concerns examining the crossing description for comments. It does not establish the later meeting experience, route decision or every access condition. Describe the useful feedback without enlarging it into an unsupported result.

items.title: Preserve missing feedback
items.body: The two other arrangements have no supplied account. Their usefulness is unknown, not automatically satisfactory or inadequate. Actual follow-up should use the relevant role and process without treating silence as a personal or group characteristic.

tabs.label: Specific learning
tabs.body: A particular care meaning changed, and Iona responded differently to Ren’s preference. This can be an intrinsic private benefit as well as inform a later appropriate task. It does not require public proof or become an assessment of the whole person.

tabs.label: Task feedback
tabs.body: The revised crossing description is useful for the supplied information task according to Ren’s account. That feedback can guide the actual next step. The later conversation and decision remain open, so the account should not claim an adopted route or complete access result.

tabs.label: Unsupported completion claim
tabs.body: Calling every arrangement successful because one task received feedback makes the evidence broader than it is. Declaring the unreported arrangements failures makes a different unsupported inference. Preserve each task’s supplied account and unanswered conditions instead.

check.question: Which account is accurate at this point?
check.correct: A particular care meaning and response changed, Ren supplied task feedback, and the later conversation and unreported arrangements remain open.
wrong: The course establishes complete intercultural mastery and legal compliance.
One useful description proves that every support arrangement succeeded.
Missing feedback proves that the other people resisted support.
check.feedbackCorrect: This preserves the actual learning and task feedback without inventing a wider outcome or explaining silence.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Mastery and legal compliance are not established by the learning case. One description’s usefulness cannot prove every arrangement. Missing feedback gives no basis for a resistance conclusion. A precise account can recognize progress and retain open questions together.

jobAid.title: Understand the person beyond an assumed disability story
jobAid.subtitle: Connect learned meaning, actual task, useful support and the responsible process.
jobAid.intro: Use Ren’s supplied an example or an appropriate question within your actual role. No medical record or personal disclosure is needed.

sections.heading: Separate account from interpretation
items: What does the person want to contribute or understand? What support have they actually requested?
Which meaning of disability, care or participation have you supplied from your own experience? You may examine it privately.
Do not infer preference, capacity, motive or safety from a diagnosis, appearance, accent, identity or disability category.

sections.heading: Understand the actual meaning and task
items: Learn individually meanings the people describe without requiring a person to represent a community or disclose a medical history.
Examine the particular task and environment: information format, timing, participation route and support. An offered feature is not proof of effectiveness.
Understanding a meaning does not require agreement with a harmful assumption or waiver of actual rights. Preserve chosen participation and relevant responsibilities.

sections.heading: Use the actual responsible process
items: A learning conversation does not approve a service, decide eligibility, release records or establish legal compliance.
For an employment accommodation request, promptly forward to the appropriate decision maker and simultaneously tell the requestor who that person is. Actual agency delegation matters.
Supervisors/managers must not request medical information or documentation; appropriate requests belong to the agency ADA Coordinator. Protect actual need-to-know information.

Managers/supervisors immediately report protected-class allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow actual procedures. Do not wait for optional learning or a proof threshold.

sections.heading: Describe learning and effects accurately
items: Name the particular meaning reconsidered and the changed response. Do not assign an intercultural stage or score.
Separate a proposed support, confirmed arrangement and observed experience. Preserve missing feedback and unresolved conditions.
Use the example, a suitable draft, or a private reflection. You do not need to share medical or personal information.

remember: Disability is not a complete account of a person’s purpose or capacity.
Learned meanings can influence interpretation without determining a group’s preferences.
Care and participation need the person’s actual account.
A support request and its formal process are different from cultural disclosure.
Native American and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA.
